name: Lena Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for doing this, Lena. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Right now I'm on a transmission crew for Northgate Energy, building a new high-voltage line out to a wind farm in the hills. We meet at the laydown yard at half six, which is just a gravel lot full of steel and cable drums, and drive out to whatever tower we're on. I'm an apprentice, so I'm mostly on the ground: sorting hardware, running the tagline, helping set up the pulling rig when we string the conductor, which is the actual wire. On a good day I get to climb with Mo, the journeyman who's teaching me.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I ran software projects for an insurance company for 22 years and burned out completely at 54. I had good savings and stock from that job, so I took a year off, and I kept watching the line crews outside our cabin after a storm and thinking they looked like the happiest people I'd ever seen. My wife Marit, she teaches pottery, told me to stop talking about it and apply. I still use AI every day, mostly to quiz myself on rigging and to log my climb times, which the crew finds hilarious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say, a bit sheepishly, that I expected more. At the yard I'd say good, nobody's job is at risk, let's get on with stringing wire. Online I'd post something about how we wasted a lot of money and electricity on a bubble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means very little changes for me. I keep learning the trade, I keep using AI as a study buddy, and I work until I'm 65 or my shoulders give out. Part of me would be a bit disappointed, because I thought these tools could help with dangerous work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena keeps going with her apprenticeship and her daily AI quizzing. She'd keep pushing Northgate's safety office to try out the drone inspection tool they've been sitting on, and she'd keep her investments as they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a small sting of disappointment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why disappointment? Most people would be relieved.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've watched Mo climb a tower in forty-knot wind to look at one bolt. If a drone or a little robot could do that, I'd be thrilled. Hype that goes nowhere means he keeps taking that risk for no reason.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd post about wasting electricity. Is that something you care about in your work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Very much. We're building lines to get wind power into the grid, and meanwhile data centres are eating up power for chatbots that mostly write emails. If it all turns out to be hype, I'd want someone to answer for that.

S0.say: I'd say, a bit sheepishly, that I expected more, and that it's good nobody's job is at risk. Online I'd post that we wasted a lot of money and electricity on a bubble.
S0.think: Privately little changes: she keeps learning the trade, uses AI as a study buddy and works until about 65. Part of her is disappointed, because she hoped these tools would help with dangerous work.
S0.do: Keeps going with her apprenticeship and daily AI quizzing. Keeps pushing Northgate's safety office to trial the drone inspection tool and leaves her investments as they are.
S0.feel: Calm, with a small sting of disappointment.
S0.quote: Hype that goes nowhere means he keeps taking that risk for no reason.
S0.fieldNote: Lena flips the usual reaction: she's disappointed that AI fizzles, because she hoped it would take risk off her mentor. She uses AI daily as a learning aid. Her progressive anger is aimed at wasted electricity, not at the technology as such.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where we have to make sure the gains get shared. At work I'd say let's get ahead of it and ask for the training. Online I'd share stuff about shorter working weeks and about the union having a say in how the new tools come in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fine, and slightly excited. I'm a beginner who's good with software, which is an odd combination on a line crew. If they bring in drones, smart sensors or a robot arm for the hot work, I might be the apprentice who's actually useful for once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena would volunteer for every pilot project Northgate ran, starting with drone inspections, and get her drone pilot's licence in the first six months, paying the 1,200 herself if the company wouldn't. She'd also go to union meetings and ask for a written deal that any time saved by new tools turns into safer crews, not smaller ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit energised. The only knot in my stomach is about the guys who hate screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are the guys who hate screens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's Ray, who's been doing this 34 years and can tell you a bad insulator by the sound it makes. He won't touch the tablet. If they start measuring people by how fast they log jobs, Ray looks slow, and he's the best lineman I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're a progressive who'd jump at the new tools. Do you ever feel those pull in different directions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: All the time. I want the tools, and I want the people who don't want them to be protected. I think that's only a contradiction if you let the company decide alone.

S1.say: I'd say we have to make sure the gains get shared. At work I'd say let's get ahead of it and ask for training, and online I'd share posts about shorter working weeks and union say over new tools.
S1.think: Privately she'd be fine and a little excited, as a beginner who's good with software. If drones, sensors or robot arms arrive, she might finally be the useful apprentice.
S1.do: Volunteers for every Northgate pilot project, starting with drone inspections, and gets a drone pilot's licence in six months, paying the 1,200 herself if needed. Asks the union for a written deal that time saved means safer crews, not smaller ones.
S1.feel: Calm and energised, with a knot of worry for colleagues who dislike screens.
S1.quote: If they start measuring people by how fast they log jobs, Ray looks slow, and he's the best lineman I know.
S1.fieldNote: Lena sees opportunity in her unusual mix of beginner skills and tech comfort. Her concern focuses on veteran colleagues like Ray who could be judged unfairly by new metrics. She resolves the tension between enthusiasm and protection by insisting workers share in decisions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to share this out fairly, right now, or it gets ugly. I'd be online a lot, and at the union, saying the companies that own the AI should pay into a fund for everyone who loses work. I wouldn't be saying stop it, because I don't think you can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm in about the safest spot you can be. I've got savings, stock and a paid-off house, and I'd be 60. I could stop tomorrow. What scares me is what happens to everyone else in two years, with no plan, and what kind of politics that brings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena would ask Northgate to put her on the team that sets up and checks the robot crews, because she knows the trade a little and software a lot. She'd give time to the union and to a campaign for a public fund paid for by AI companies. If the robot work wasn't there for her, she'd retire at 60 without much fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for myself, but properly frightened for the country. It's a strange split.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years' warning, what does the short time change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally, it barely matters, I have enough. But two years is no time for Ray or for the 25-year-olds on our crew. With that little warning, I'd stop worrying about my career and put my energy into the politics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Marit that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're lucky, and I'd feel a bit guilty saying it. Then we'd probably talk about who in our family needs help, because Marit's brother drives a delivery van and he'd be first in line to lose his job.

S2.say: I'd say we need to share this out fairly right now or it gets ugly. Online and at the union I'd argue that AI companies should pay into a fund for everyone who loses work, rather than trying to stop it.
S2.think: Privately she's in about the safest position possible, with savings, stock and a paid-off house at 60. What scares her is the effect on everyone else with no plan, and the politics that follows.
S2.do: Asks Northgate to put her on the team setting up and checking robot crews. Gives time to the union and to a campaign for an AI-funded public fund, and retires at 60 if no role exists.
S2.feel: Uneasy for herself but properly frightened for the country, a split she finds strange.
S2.quote: I'd say we're lucky, and I'd feel a bit guilty saying it.
S2.fieldNote: Lena is open about how secure she is, and her fear is almost entirely for others. Two years makes her drop career thinking and turn to politics. Her instinct is to shape and share the change, not stop it, which sets her apart from more resistant progressives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to build a proper plan, so let's build it. I'd push the union to sit down with Northgate now about which jobs change and what training people get. Online I'd keep beating the drum for a public fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is kind of perfect for me. I'd finish my apprenticeship, then move into robot supervision or drone work, which uses both halves of my brain. I'd be 63 and still useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena would finish her apprenticeship in two years, then take a robotics technician course at the technical college, about a year of evenings. She'd pitch Northgate on a role checking robot crews in the field. She'd also help run union workshops teaching older lineworkers to use the new tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and honestly a little excited. Five years feels like enough to do it well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd teach older lineworkers. Would Ray come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not at first. He'd come if I bribed him with coffee and promised not to say the word app. I'd want him there more than anyone, because he'd tell the robot people what they got wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the robot crew job look like, in your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone standing at the bottom of the tower with a tablet, watching the robot do the bolts and the clamps, and a person with real line sense saying stop when something's off. That's where I'd want to be. I don't know if it'll look like that, but that's my guess.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to build a proper plan, so let's build it. I'd push the union to sit down with Northgate now and keep calling for a public fund online.
S3.think: Privately five years suits her: she finishes her apprenticeship, then moves into robot supervision or drone work. She'd be 63 and still useful.
S3.do: Finishes her apprenticeship in two years, then takes a year of evening robotics technician classes at the technical college. Pitches Northgate on a field role checking robot crews and helps run union workshops for older lineworkers.
S3.feel: Calm and a little excited, since five years feels like enough to do it well.
S3.quote: He'd come if I bribed him with coffee and promised not to say the word app.
S3.fieldNote: Five years is Lena's sweet spot: enough to qualify and move into the new kind of work. She imagines a concrete job at the bottom of the tower with a tablet, while admitting she can't know. She wants veterans like Ray in the room because they'd catch what the robot makers miss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is the best version of this, so there's no excuse for anyone being left behind. I'd say it at the union, at Northgate's safety meetings and online. I'd also say the AI companies should start paying in now, not in 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be 68 by then, so I'd do a few good years and then step back. It barely threatens me. What I'd think about is my son Erik, who's a nurse, and whether ten years is enough to protect jobs like his.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena would finish her apprenticeship, work as a journeywoman for a few years and take on drone and robot work as it comes in. She'd retire around 65, before AGI lands, and spend part of her time volunteering with the union's training programme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Curious, even. I'd get to see the start of it and leave before the hard part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does that compare with two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At two years I'm a bystander who's lucky and guilty. At ten I'm part of building it. I'd much rather be in the second one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Erik?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To get comfortable using the tools early, like I did, but also to join his union and stay loud. Nursing is the kind of job where a machine might do the charting but people still want a hand on their shoulder. I can't promise him that, though.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is the best version, so there's no excuse for anyone being left behind. I'd also say the AI companies should start paying in now, not in 2036.
S4.think: Privately she'd be 68 by then, so it barely threatens her. She thinks more about her son Erik, a nurse, and whether ten years is enough to protect jobs like his.
S4.do: Keeps going with her apprenticeship, works as a journeywoman and takes on drone and robot work as it comes. Retires around 65 and volunteers with the union's training programme.
S4.feel: Calm and curious about seeing the start of the change before leaving.
S4.quote: At two years I'm a bystander who's lucky and guilty.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Lena feels like a builder rather than a bystander. Her advice to her son mirrors her own path: use the tools early but stay organised. She is careful not to promise what she can't know about nursing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, but not for me. I'd be fine. It's the speed: Ray, the young apprentices, Marit's brother, all of them hit at once with no plan. What would help is a public fund paid for by the AI companies, real retraining money, and workers having a say in how robots come onto the crews.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask whether people want these tools at all, not just how they'd cope. I do want them, if they keep people like Mo from climbing towers in a gale. But wanting the tools and wanting the companies to own all of the gains are two very different things.

headlineQuote: I've watched Mo climb a tower in forty-knot wind to look at one bolt.
portrait: Lena Larsen ran software projects for 22 years before burning out and joining a transmission crew as an apprentice at 55. She uses AI every day to study, has savings, stock and a paid-off house, and is openly aware of how lucky that makes her. She wants AI and robots to take risk off line crews, but insists that workers share the gains and have a say. Across the scenarios she stays calm for herself, while the two-year picture frightens her for colleagues, family and the country and turns her toward politics.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, not for herself but because colleagues, young apprentices and family members would all be hit at once with no plan.
whatWouldHelp: A public fund paid for by AI companies, real retraining money, and workers having a say in how robots come onto the crews.
